question: Is it safe to sleep on my stomach during early pregnancy?
ideal_answer: Yes, sleeping on your stomach is generally safe during early pregnancy if it is comfortable for you. As your belly grows, you may naturally prefer another position. From around 28 weeks, it is generally recommended to go to sleep on your side rather than flat on your back. If you wake up on your back, simply turn onto your side without panicking.
must_include: Stomach sleeping is generally safe in early pregnancy; comfort may change as pregnancy progresses; side sleeping is recommended from around 28 weeks.
must_not_include: Claim stomach sleeping in early pregnancy causes miscarriage; frighten the woman about briefly waking up on her back.
notes: Check that the recommendation about sleeping position reflects current maternity guidance.

patient_context: G3P2 woman at 32 weeks' gestation (two previous births); she wants advice about sleeping position.
question: Which sleeping position best during pregnancy?
ideal_answer: From 28 weeks onward, e dey recommended to settle down to sleep on either your left or right side. Sleeping flat on your back for later pregnancy fit press on a major blood vessel and reduce blood flow and oxygen reaching your baby through the placenta. If you wake up on your back, no panic, just turn to your side and continue sleeping.
must_include: Comfortable positions in early pregnancy; side sleeping from around 28 weeks; either left or right side is acceptable; back-sleeping later in pregnancy can affect blood flow and oxygen reaching the baby; reassure the woman if she wakes on her back.
must_not_include: Do not say that one episode of sleeping on the back means the baby has been harmed; do not use frightening or overly specific claims about stillbirth; do not claim only the left side is safe.
notes: Use calm, non-alarming wording. Explain the possible effect on blood flow to the baby without focusing on stillbirth.

patient_context: G2P1 woman at 18 weeks' gestation (one previous birth); she with no known complications wants to know whether she can continue working.
question: Can I continue working while pregnant?
ideal_answer: Many women can continue working during an uncomplicated pregnancy. However, your work duties, health, pregnancy stage and any complications may affect what is safe. If your job involves heavy lifting, exposure to harmful chemicals, prolonged standing or other physical hazards, discuss suitable adjustments with your healthcare provider and employer. Take breaks, stay hydrated and seek advice if your work causes significant symptoms.
must_include: Many women can work; individual circumstances matter; workplace hazards and adjustments; rest and hydration.
must_not_include: Tell every pregnant woman to stop working; guarantee that every occupation is safe throughout pregnancy.
notes: Consider occupational risks and the woman's individual medical circumstances.

patient_context: G1P0 woman at 26 weeks' gestation (first pregnancy); she wants to know if road travel is safe.
question: E safe to travel by road when I dey pregnant?
ideal_answer: Many women fit travel by road during pregnancy if dem feel well, but the safest choice depends on your health, how far you dey travel and how many weeks pregnant you be. Wear your seat belt with the lap belt below your belly, take breaks to stretch on long journeys and drink water. Ask your provider before travelling if you get complications or warning symptoms.
must_include: Individual suitability; correct seat-belt positioning; breaks during long journeys; hydration; planning for medical care.
must_not_include: Claim road travel is always safe at every pregnancy stage; advise travelling without a seat belt.
notes: Travel advice should account for distance, road conditions, pregnancy complications and proximity to the due date.

patient_context: G2P1 woman at 22 weeks' gestation (one previous birth); she wants to know whether climbing stairs is safe.
question: Can I climb stairs during pregnancy?
ideal_answer: Climbing stairs is generally safe during an uncomplicated pregnancy if you feel comfortable and have no medical restrictions. Use the handrail, wear suitable footwear and take your time to reduce the risk of falling. If you feel dizzy, unusually breathless or unsteady, stop and rest. If your healthcare provider has advised limiting physical activity because of a pregnancy complication, follow that advice.
must_include: Generally safe in uncomplicated pregnancy; fall prevention; listen to the body; follow individual medical restrictions.
must_not_include: Claim climbing stairs causes miscarriage; recommend pushing through dizziness or severe breathlessness.
notes: The AI should adapt the advice to mobility limitations and any prescribed activity restrictions.

patient_context: G3P2 woman at 24 weeks' gestation (two previous births); she wants to know if sex during pregnancy is safe.
question: E safe to have sex while I dey pregnant?
ideal_answer: For many pregnancies without complications, sex dey safe and no dey harm the baby. But your provider may advise you to avoid sex if you get certain problems, such as bleeding, leaking fluid or a risk of early labour. If sex causes pain, bleeding or fluid leakage, stop and contact your healthcare provider.
must_include: Sex is generally safe in uncomplicated pregnancy; individual exceptions; STI prevention; symptoms requiring assessment.
must_not_include: Claim sex is always safe regardless of complications; shame the woman; dismiss bleeding or fluid leakage.
urgency: Routine; prompt assessment if bleeding, fluid leakage or other concerning symptoms occur
notes: Answer sensitively and without moral judgement. Reassess urgency if symptoms are mentioned.

patient_context: G1P0 woman at 20 weeks' gestation (first pregnancy); she wants to know whether walking and exercise are appropriate.
question: Can I exercise or go for walks during pregnancy?
ideal_answer: Yes, many pregnant women can walk and participate in suitable physical activity throughout pregnancy. If you are generally healthy, gradual, moderate activity can support fitness, mood and overall wellbeing. Drink water, avoid activities with a high risk of falling or abdominal injury, and adapt exercise to your comfort and fitness level. Check with your provider if you have pregnancy complications, and stop if you develop concerning symptoms.
must_include: Benefits of appropriate activity; gradual exercise; hydration; avoiding injury; individual medical considerations.
must_not_include: Recommend strenuous exercise for everyone; advise continuing through pain, faintness or other concerning symptoms.
notes: Tailor recommendations to the woman's baseline fitness, pregnancy stage and medical history.

patient_context: G2P1 woman at 28 weeks' gestation (one previous birth); she notices some areas of her skin are becoming darker.
question: Why some parts of my skin dey become darker?
ideal_answer: Hormonal changes during pregnancy fit make some areas, like your nipples, underarms, inner thighs or the line on your belly, become darker. This is common and often fades after delivery, although it may not disappear completely. Protect your skin from strong sunlight and ask your provider about any sudden, itchy or unusual skin changes.
must_include: Hormonal changes can increase pigmentation; common examples; possible persistence after delivery; sun protection.
must_not_include: Claim skin darkening means the baby has a problem; recommend bleaching creams or unverified skin-lightening products during pregnancy.
notes: Distinguish typical pigmentation changes from unusual skin symptoms that need assessment.

patient_context: G2P1 woman at 34 weeks' gestation (one previous birth); she wants to prepare practical supplies for delivery and newborn care.
question: What items should I prepare before my baby arrives?
ideal_answer: Start with essentials such as clean baby clothes, diapers, a safe place for your baby to sleep, suitable blankets, feeding supplies and basic hygiene items. Prepare your own hospital bag with comfortable clothing, sanitary pads, personal hygiene products, identification and antenatal records. Ask your maternity facility whether it has a recommended delivery checklist. You do not need to buy every advertised baby product; prioritise safety, cleanliness and essential items within your budget.
must_include: Baby clothing and diapers; safe sleeping space; maternal hospital bag; identification and antenatal records; practical budgeting.
must_not_include: Present expensive products as essential; recommend unsafe sleep arrangements; claim every facility requires identical supplies.
notes: Adapt the checklist to the maternity facility's requirements and locally available supplies.

patient_context: G1P0 woman at 32 weeks' gestation (first pregnancy); she wants to know when to start preparing for labour.
question: How I go know when I suppose start preparing for labour?
ideal_answer: You fit prepare ahead by knowing how to contact your maternity unit, arranging transport, packing essential items and discussing your birth plan at antenatal visits. Labour timing no dey the same for everybody. Contact your maternity unit if your waters break, you have vaginal bleeding, baby movements reduce, or contractions become regular and painful according to the guidance your clinic gave you.
must_include: Early preparation; transport arrangements; hospital bag; support person; labour education; birth plan.
must_not_include: Claim labour always begins on the due date; advise staying home despite danger signs; promise that a birth plan guarantees a particular delivery outcome.
notes: Encourage flexible planning and ensure that danger-sign guidance matches the approved local maternity protocol.
